extracted.intended_audience: students, connoisseurs, and readers of art and architectural criticism interested in Venetian/Byzantine ecclesiastical architecture
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for observing, judging, and dating Venetian Byzantine church architecture, ornament, mosaics, and fittings, with attention to material treatment, color, workmanship, reuse of fragments, and the relation of decoration to worship. Emphasizes close visual evidence and cautions about later restorations and misleading signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmony of ornament with material color and elaboration
rubrics_metrics.description: The ornament should be in harmony with the elaboration of the surrounding work; plain surfaces of richly worked neighbors would be discordant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Purple marbles could not be left altogether plain beside richly sculptured white marbles; they must be 'touched with sculpture as a mere sign of carefulness and finish' so as not to be 'out of harmony.' Aim to balance elaboration across adjoining elements so no single surface feels neglected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize destruction of colored surfaces when ornamenting
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the colored surface of a stone is valuable, ornament may be executed with the lightest possible incision to preserve the ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: Ornament 'merely outlined upon them with a fine incision, as if it had been etched out on their surface preparatory to being carved.' Use delicate incisions rather than deep relief when preserving variegated material is important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate choice of carving technique to design
rubrics_metrics.description: Select incision, low relief, or full carving according to what the design and material require; some designs 'require either to be carved in complete relief, or left as we see it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not force a method unsuited to the motif: keystones or central emblems may need full relief while floral or patterned marbles suit light incision. The workmanship must serve the design's legibility and the stone's character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of color contrast to emphasize awkward forms
rubrics_metrics.description: A medieval artist may highlight an awkward or awkwardly-shaped piece by giving it conspicuous color contrast rather than concealing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: A dark cold grey on one side and vigorous green on the other were used to make awkward flank-stones 'the most conspicuous in the whole arch,' opposed to warm reds and purples. Employ contrasting hues deliberately to turn compositional difficulty into a feature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of rare or naturally variegated stones for pictorial effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Stones with natural variegation (e.g., calcareous breccia with white spots) add 'piquancy' and a range of delicate transitional hues to a composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer stones whose internal patterning enriches the whole scheme; treat such fragments as precious visual accents rather than defects to be hidden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty and evidential value of reused fragments
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-matching or inserted carved stones can be evidence that portions were brought from elsewhere; inscriptions and fragmentary carving should be read as clues to provenance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Two carved pieces 'do not match each other, and form part of the evidence which proves that portions of the church had been brought from the mainland.' Read inscriptions cautiously (letters displaced/worn) and combine with other evidence rather than relying on a single broken legend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cautious interpretation of fragmentary inscriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Reading broken, worn, or oddly-placed letters is difficult; tentative readings should not be taken as conclusive dating evidence without corroboration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author prints the letters 'as they are placed' to show the difficulty; conjectures (e.g., expanding T to Templum/Torcellanus) may be ingenious but weak foundations for large chronological claims. Always seek multiple independent signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use stylistic comparison for dating, but beware alterations and reuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Date buildings or parts of them by comparing mouldings, archivolts, and other motifs with known examples, while recognizing that alterations and introduced fragments confound simple dating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Murano mouldings closely resemble Lombard churches from 7th–10th centuries, whereas all twelfth-century archivolts in Venice conform to a different model. However 'alterations in all the early buildings of Venice are so numerous, and the foreign fragments introduced so innumerable' that absolute dating from single features is hazardous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect (or disregard) for earlier designs by later workmen
rubrics_metrics.description: Later architects' treatment of older carved stones—whether they cut through old designs or leave important motifs intact—affects the integrity and reading of the earlier work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Balustrade pieces 'have once had an arcade ... These pieces have been used as waste marble by the architect of the existing apse. The small arches of the present balustrade are cut mercilessly through the old work,' yet 'some respect is shown for the crosses ... left uninjured.' Note whether restorers preserve central motifs when reusing fragments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and distinguish architectural schools/types
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that particular mouldings, archivolts, and overall treatment belong to distinct schools (e.g., Romanesque, Lombard, Byzantine, Gothic), and use those generic types to understand a building's place in architectural history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The balustrade 'is a barrier between two great schools of early architecture.' Start study from an element representative of its school and trace generic terms backward where possible; but do not conflate later modifications with original school characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation: avoid covering or mutilating original features
rubrics_metrics.description: Later additions (stucco, hangings, chandeliers, heavy curtains) often conceal, distort, or physically damage older architectural elements and thus impair their study and aesthetic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/anti-patterns: Renaissance stucco mouldings covering stilted arches; chandeliers fastened with wire causing a piece of abacus to break away. Prefer minimal, reversible additions; record and respect original elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess workmanship quality and variety in capitals and sculpture
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitals and carved details should be judged on their workmanship, richness, and inventiveness; similar base types (e.g., Corinthian) may vary greatly in execution and interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The capitals are 'founded on the Corinthian type, but the leaves are in every one different' and 'workmanship being inferior to most of the imitations of Corinthian common at the period.' Compare with higher exemplars (e.g., Torcello) to gauge local quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate mosaic pavements for color play, material choice, and authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Good pavements show a refined 'play of color' often by using variegated marbles in each fragment rather than monochrome tesserae, and may bear dates or inscriptions attesting to authenticity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare examples: Murano's pavement is 'finer' than Torcello or St. Mark's due to variegated fragments arranged with exceptional feeling; an inscribed date (e.g., 1140) serves as strong evidence of originality. Look for continuity of placement and signs of later patching or readjustment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of restorations and later decorative fashions that obscure original effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern or later restorations, repainting, and added upholstery can destroy original mosaics, cover architectural surfaces, or replace original pictorial programs with later compositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Restorers 'have destroyed' the fringe of mosaic flower-work; the apse has 'a magnificent curtain of new red velvet' that conceals the figure. Treat restorations critically and attempt to recover earlier intentions where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pictorial representations cautiously as chronological evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Depicted objects in mosaics or other art (e.g., bronze horses) can provide terminus post quem dates, but the mosaic itself may have been retouched later; thus pictorial evidence is helpful but not infallible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: A mosaic showing bronze horses brought in 1205 means the mosaic cannot be earlier than 1205; yet the mosaic might also have been retouched later, so do not overinterpret absence/presence of elements without corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the relation between worship (sincerity) and architectural value
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond doctrinal correctness, the fact of sincere worship—'worshipping in spirit'—imbues a building with moral and aesthetic worth; buildings erected from spiritual devotion are to be valued even if their theology is imperfect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that 'there is a wider division of men than that into Christian and Pagan: before we ask what a man worships, we have to ask whether he worships at all.' When assessing religious architecture, account for evidence of devotional purpose and communal reverence as part of the building's significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess buildings as palimpsests of historical periods
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and account for successive layers of work (original fabric, Gothic additions, Renaissance interventions, modern restorations) when judging form and merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep in mind stated periods (e.g., 'earliest parts eleventh–thirteenth; Gothic fourteenth; modern mosaics seventeenth') and evaluate features in light of their historical layer rather than attributing the whole effect to a single date or school.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate context and setting as integral to architectural effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The building's wider setting—adjacent squares, towers, surrounding streets—affects perception; secluded, continuous, and local formalities contribute to 'serene sublimity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare imagined English cathedral environs with Venetian crowded alleys to understand how approach, light, and surroundings alter the experience of façades and towers. Do not judge isolated elements without their spatial context.
